newsitem.title: GERMANY: Passenger ship insurance too low - marine expert.
newsitem.headline: Passenger ship insurance too low - marine expert.

text.p: A serious passenger ship accident could cost the insurance industry $4.0 billion and premiums needed to rise to reflect this, a leading German marine insurance expert said on Saturday.

The high liability potential of such risks will in the long run lead to massive increases in insurance premiums, Dr Harald Zeller, until December Munich Re's deputy head of marine insurance, and now head of consultancy firm Zeller Associates, said.
"Accidents involving cruise vessels or ferries are a permanent large risk," the master mariner and lawyer told a conference on ocean hull insurance, organised by the Bremen Nautical Association.

A large, fully occupied passenger ship formed a "giant risk potential," said Zeller. "Up to 3,360 passengers on board plus crew form a critical mass, which is very difficult to handle in a normal situation, let alone in an emergency," he added.

"This is partly due to the unfamiliar environment and the consumption of nicotine and alcohol," he said, adding that even with a first rate crew the sheer number of people involved posed a serious problem.
In the U.S., courts had made awards of three to four million dollars for airline passengers who died in accidents, he noted.
"If in a passenger ship accident 1,000 or 1,200 people die, you have claims of gigantic proportions." To that, the loss of the ship had to be added.
The main risk with cruise vessels was not the sinking of the ship, but fire on board, Zeller said.

Ferries had an "in-built instability of design, which can lead to a rapid total loss in case of water entering the ship, either because of a collision or due to a stranding following navigational errors."

Zeller said it would be wrong for the German market to under-estimate such risks. There had been some near-misses in recent years, and the market should also look to the Baltic and the severe accidents that happened there, for example the sinking of the Estonia.
Insurance premiums for large marine risks were too low, he said. In the long run, especially reinsurers would ask for increased prices.
